❯ Write a 400 word essay about tmux, in chat only, no tools.

  Thought for 14s

● tmux

  tmux is a terminal multiplexer. It lets you run several terminal sessions inside one window, detach from them, and
  reattach later from the same machine or a different one. Nicholas Marriott released it in 2007 as a more maintainable
  alternative to GNU Screen. It is now installed by default, or one package away, on nearly every Unix-like system.

  It has three levels. A session holds one or more windows, and each window can be split into panes, each running its
  own shell or program. A tmux server process owns all of this, which is why everything keeps running when your terminal
  closes. You control it with a prefix key, Ctrl-b by default, followed by a command key. The prefix then % splits a
  pane, and the prefix then d detaches.

  Persistence is the main reason people use it. If you work over SSH and the connection drops, a plain shell dies and
  takes your running job with it. Inside tmux, the job keeps running on the server. You reconnect, run tmux attach, and
  find everything as you left it. That makes it useful for long builds, database migrations, and any process you want to
  check on later without keeping a laptop open.

  It also organizes local work. Many developers keep one session per project, with windows for an editor, a test runner,
  and logs. Named sessions make switching quick. Because tmux is scriptable, a short shell script using new-session and
  split-window, or a tool like tmuxinator or tmuxp, can rebuild a whole workspace in one command.

  Configuration lives in ~/.tmux.conf. Common changes include remapping the prefix to Ctrl-a, enabling mouse support,
  starting window numbering at 1, and customizing the status line. Plugins managed through TPM add features such as
  saving and restoring sessions across reboots.

  tmux has costs. The prefix model takes a few days to learn, copy mode has its own keybindings, and clipboard
  integration and true color often need extra configuration. Modern terminal emulators with built-in tabs and splits
  cover some of the same ground for local use. None of them match detach and reattach on a remote server.

  For anyone who works on remote machines or juggles many terminal tasks, tmux is still worth learning.
